To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) The genome-wide search for alcoholism susceptibility genes in a large, well-characterized sample of male twins from the Collaborative Study on the Genetics of Alcoholism (COGA) identified a region on chromosome 7 that is associated with the level of response to a single dose of alcohol, and 2) the same region was found to be associated with alcoholism in the same sample.

1) The low level of response (LLR) phenotype, defined as a low level of alcohol consumption in response to the alcohol challenge, was significantly associated with a 3-cM region on the distal long arm of chromosome 1, and 2) the LLR phenotype was also significantly associated with a region on the short arm of chromosome 4.
the genes encoding alcohol dehydrogenase 1B and 1C, and the aldehyde dehydrogenase gene are associated with low alcohol response in a Japanese population.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of genetic factors that relate to a person's response to alcohol.
the genetic and molecular basis of alcoholism.
the identification of genes that influence the level of response to ethanol.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
alcohol is a complex drug that can cause both beneficial and detrimental health effects.
there is no evidence to support the use of alcohol for the treatment of any medical condition.
the low level of response is a complex trait that has a genetic component.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified a region on chromosome 1 that contains a gene (or genes) that is involved in determining an individual's response to alcohol.
we found no genes that were consistently associated with low response to alcohol in the 5 studies we have conducted.
we found no genes or genetic variants that are related to the low level of response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the genome-wide association study (GWAS) approach has great potential for the identification of genes that influence alcohol response.
we can now use genetic data to identify individuals who are more likely to be alcohol dependent, and this can inform the design of prevention and intervention programs.
there are genetic factors that influence alcohol response and that these genetic factors are not necessarily the same as the genetic factors that influence the risk of developing alcoholism.
